core: Working definition: essential fatty acids are fats the body cannot make on its own and that must come from food (attributed to standard nutrition-science framing, e.g., NIH ODS fact sheets)
The two families: omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acids, each named with one line and original food examples
Why they matter: cell membranes, inflammation regulation (eicosanoids), brain development (DHA)
Deficiency is rare: most diets provide enough (the honest note, with symptoms stated factually)
Food sources: fish, walnuts, flaxseed, vegetable oils
Balance idea: both families matter, stated simply, no dosing
Honest framing: 'essential' means needed from food, not that more is better
supporting: ALA, EPA, and DHA as the main omega-3s; linoleic acid as the main essential omega-6
Eicosanoids as signaling molecules built from both families
Limited ALA-to-EPA/DHA conversion as background for why direct food sources matter
No established optimal omega-6 to omega-3 ratio
outOfScope: Fats in general (own sibling topic: nutrition:foundations:fats)
Saturated versus unsaturated fat chemistry and health effects (own sibling topic: nutrition:foundations:saturated-and-unsaturated-fat)
Omega-3/omega-6 supplements, doses, and supplementation claims (own sibling topic: nutrition:foundations:supplements)
Detailed lipid biochemistry and cell-biology depth (other subjects, reference only)

claims.claim: Essential fatty acids are fats the body cannot make on its own, so they must come from food; the two families are the omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acids.
Only ALA (omega-3) and linoleic acid (omega-6) are strictly essential; the body converts only limited amounts of ALA into EPA and DHA (reported conversion under 15%).
Omega-3s and omega-6s are components of the phospholipids that form cell membranes; DHA in particular is concentrated in the retina and brain.
Both families are used to form eicosanoids, signaling molecules that help regulate inflammation, blood vessel tone, and blood clotting.
DHA accumulates in the brain and retina most rapidly during the third trimester of pregnancy, and sufficient long-chain omega-3s during pregnancy matter for fetal growth and neurodevelopment.

Food sources: ALA in flaxseed, walnuts, chia seeds, and canola and soybean oils; EPA and DHA in cold-water fatty fish such as salmon, mackerel, herring, and sardines; omega-6 linoleic acid in sunflower, safflower, corn, and soybean oils.
Essential fatty acid deficiency can cause rough, scaly skin and dermatitis, but it is very rare in the United States; most people get enough ALA from the foods they eat.
Both families are essential and neither should be avoided; researchers have not defined an optimal omega-6 to omega-3 ratio, and ratio-based recommendations are contested.

positions: Some researchers propose that the relative intakes of omega-6s and omega-3s matter for chronic disease risk
Others argue ratio measures are too nonspecific, and the optimal ratio has not been defined
Marketing language often treats omega-3 as the only 'good' essential family and omega-6 as something to avoid
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states factually that both families are essential, that neither should be avoided, and that no optimal ratio or dose is established; it makes no ratio or dosing recommendation.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Which fatty acids count as essential
positions: Strictly, only ALA and linoleic acid are essential because the body cannot make them at all
EPA and DHA are often called essential in consumer materials even though the body can convert small amounts of ALA into them
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson names ALA and linoleic acid as the strictly essential fatty acids, notes that ALA-to-EPA/DHA conversion is limited, and explains why direct food sources therefore matter — without labeling EPA/DHA 'non-essential.'

conflictingEvidence.issue: How common essential fatty acid deficiency actually is
positions: Deficiency produces real symptoms (rough, scaly skin, dermatitis) and can occur in extreme cases such as severe fat restriction
In the United States, omega-3 deficiency is very rare and most people get enough ALA from food
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the symptoms factually and pairs them with the honest note that most diets provide enough, avoiding both alarm and dismissal.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft described essential fatty acids as a generic 'foundational concept' used mainly as a study-skill building block (define/apply/limits) with no nutritional content — not supported by any source and discarded.
The draft's vocabulary treated 'context' and 'evidence' as the core terms of the topic — not supported; replaced with the actual fatty-acid terms.
The draft's Eli-10 'toolbox drawer' analogy — generic boilerplate, not supported by any source, replaced.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced all machine-generated boilerplate with source-verified content: working definition, omega-3 and omega-6 families, roles, deficiency rarity, food sources, and the balance idea.
Corrected the framing so 'essential' is taught as 'needed from food because the body cannot make it' rather than as a vague quality rating.
Added the honest note (NIH ODS consumer sheet) that most people in the U.S. get enough ALA and that omega-3 deficiency is very rare, while still stating the real deficiency symptoms.
Kept supplements and dosing out of scope per sibling-topic ownership (nutrition:foundations:supplements).
rightsIssues: None — all four sources are used reference-only; no source wording is reproduced in the lesson.

sourceRecords.title: Omega-3 Fatty Acids: Fact Sheet for Health Professionals
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly 2026-08-22. Supports: ALA and linoleic acid are essential fatty acids that must be obtained from the diet; omega-3s are components of cell-membrane phospholipids; DHA is concentrated in the retina and brain and accumulates most rapidly in the third trimester of pregnancy; eicosanoids are signaling molecules with wide-ranging functions; ALA-to-EPA/DHA conversion is under 15%; ALA sources include flaxseed, chia seeds, walnuts, and canola and soybean oils, while cold-water fatty fish (salmon, mackerel, herring, sardines) supply EPA and DHA; deficiency of essential fatty acids can cause rough, scaly skin and dermatitis; the optimal omega-6/omega-3 ratio has not been defined.

sourceRecords.title: Omega-3 Fatty Acids: An Essential Contribution
sourceRecords.provider: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, The Nutrition Source
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly 2026-08-22. Supports: DHA is the most abundant fatty acid in the brain; omega-6 fats are also essential, are a critical part of the structure of every cell, and are building blocks for hormones that regulate inflammation, blood vessel narrowing, and blood clotting; most Americans take in far more omega-6 than omega-3; the omega-3/omega-6 ratio is contested and no optimal value is established; walnuts and flaxseed are ALA sources.
